title: Perception, grouping, and information hierarchy
outcome: Use proximity, similarity, alignment, and contrast to make the page’s structure understandable.
useCase: Dense dashboards and responsive ticket pages.
benefits: Reduces search effort without removing needed information.
drawbacks: Grouping can mislead if it implies a relationship the behavior does not honor.
version: Web UX · WCAG 2.2 · principles, not magic formulas
cue: Group by meaning. Emphasize by task.

trace.title: Primary question
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

People scan before they read closely. Visual grouping suggests relationships.

Nearby controls look related. Similar styling suggests similar purpose.

A border around a group can imply a shared context. These are useful perceptual tendencies, not rules that override every task.

Give the page a primary question. A ticket page might answer “What needs attention now?” Use headings and spacing to distinguish queue context, the main record, and secondary details.

If every element is bright and bold, none has priority.

Visual order and keyboard/reading order should agree. CSS can move a button visually while leaving its document position confusing.

Use semantic headings and a sensible source order. Do not make color the only signal for priority or failure.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Ask a person to point to the current queue, the selected ticket, the primary next action, and unsaved state. Do they infer the intended relationships without a tutorial?

Then remove color from the sketch and test reading order by keyboard. Grouping should still be understandable.

A decorative divider is not a replacement for a meaningful heading.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: Large gaps inside a field and small gaps between unrelated fields can imply the wrong grouping. A floating global action can look as if it applies only to the nearest item.

recallPrompt: Without notes: Use proximity, similarity, alignment, and contrast to make the page’s structure understandable. Explain one example and one failure.
